lessons.title: Prose is a hope; only something that fires is a fix
lessons.text: A rule that only lives in a document is a hope. Every recurring failure gets a check that fires on its own — a scheduled job, a CI gate, a hook, or a test — and the fix is not done until that check exists.

lessons.title: Built is not wired; correctness and activation are separate claims
lessons.text: Shipping code is not the same as activating it. A guard that is written and tested but never registered protects nothing, so wiring is verified as its own step.

lessons.title: Watchdogs enumerate, never sample, and measure their own coverage
lessons.text: A monitor that samples will eventually report green over the part it did not look at. Checks enumerate their whole inventory from the live system and fail when their own coverage shrinks.

lessons.title: A tool that silently does less than asked fails in the unsafe direction
lessons.text: A command that accepts an option it does not implement reports success while doing less. Unknown flags are errors, and "could not measure" is never displayed the way a real number is.

lessons.title: Green locally and green in CI are evidence about the build, never the deploy
lessons.text: "CI is green" describes the build, not what users are running. Every release is verified by reading the live surface afterward, and a green pipeline is never the last step.

lessons.title: Constant and graceful fallbacks convert failures into silence
lessons.text: A graceful fallback is a silent failure with better manners. Missing data is reported, never replaced by a plausible default that hides how often the gap occurs.

lessons.title: A monitor is only as good as the assertions it still contains
lessons.text: A health check that returns "ok" over an empty list of assertions is worse than none. Monitors are verified for shape and freshness, not just for having run.

lessons.title: Copy the value, never the label; a comment's safety claim is testable
lessons.text: The label on a thing and the value inside it drift apart. Billing, trial length, and configuration are read from the value the system actually enforces, and any comment claiming "this is safe" gets a test.

lessons.title: Shared-infrastructure failures wear the costume of code bugs
lessons.text: When many pipelines share one machine or one budget, an outage looks like a code failure. A monitor establishes whether a red result is fixable by any commit before it files work against the code.

lessons.title: A test double must refuse what the real system refuses
lessons.text: A stand-in used for testing has to say no wherever the real system says no. If it is more permissive, every test passes and the live system still refuses, which is the hardest kind of gap to see.

lessons.title: A fix applied to a list covers that day's list; corrections must copy to twins
lessons.text: A fix applied to the repositories you remembered protects only those. Fleet-wide changes are applied from a live enumeration and re-checked on a schedule, and a diagnosis on one job is applied to every job with the same shape.

lessons.title: Two package managers means two truths; declare dependencies and sync both sides
lessons.text: When a project installs with one package manager locally and another in production, a class of bug is invisible on one side by construction. Dependencies are declared explicitly and both lockfiles are kept in step by a check, not by discipline.

lessons.title: Test the wiring, not only the logic
lessons.text: A test suite that builds its own inputs can pass while the real caller passes zeros. Tests read what the system actually produces, and a safety gate that has never fired is checked for what it receives.

lessons.title: A bug that survives repair was diagnosed at the wrong layer
lessons.text: If the same bug keeps coming back after a fix, the fix is at the wrong layer. Measure outward from the symptom until a number stops matching instead of repairing what is visible.

lessons.title: Irreversible actions get a refusal at the tool boundary, not a rule in prose
lessons.text: Anything irreversible — deleting production data, deleting a branch with unmerged work, granting an automation new authority — is blocked at the command boundary, not by a policy people are expected to remember.

lessons.title: Stage explicit paths; shared scratch state is hostile
lessons.text: Staging "everything" eventually commits a secret. Commits stage named paths, and anything several processes can write to is treated as untrusted.

lessons.title: Multi-writer stores need merge and recovery paths tested against the state failures actually produce
lessons.text: A log that only ever appends must be merged as a log, or a merge will quietly drop the newest line. Sync failure paths are tested against the broken state they really produce, and silent loss is treated as worse than a visible conflict.

lessons.title: An approval gate must cover every path to the terminal state
lessons.text: An approval gate that checks one path lets the other paths through. Anything that publishes in someone's name is re-read on a schedule and reverted if it lacks the approval, whichever route it took.

lessons.title: One metric has one owner; delegate to the reconciler, never re-derive
lessons.text: Two internally consistent systems can disagree at the seam. Every headline metric has exactly one computation that other surfaces call, and each reader is asked which sources it might be missing.

lessons.title: Detection without delivery is not detection
lessons.text: A monitor that fires into a channel nobody reads has not fired. Every signal goes to the one surface its reader actually looks at, with dedupe, and a signal source that stops updating is itself an alert.

lessons.title: Pre-committed decisions need a detector like outages do
lessons.text: A decision rule written in a document slips on the day it matters. Thresholds are evaluated by a scheduled job against live data and surfaced to the decider, not left for someone to remember to check.

lessons.title: Count before assuming headroom, and look for the mechanism that already works
lessons.text: Free quotas are shared across an account, so the headroom is counted, never assumed. Before building a replacement, check whether a working mechanism already exists.

lessons.title: Own the artifact, not the platform's interpretation of your exit code
lessons.text: A release gate must control whether the artifact exists, not merely return a failing status another system may or may not honor. Gates are proven by forcing a failure live and confirming nothing shipped.

lessons.title: Empowerment first: an owner item naming a credential records the paths tried without one
lessons.text: Before asking a person for access, exhaust what the machine already holds — an authenticated CLI counts. A request for credentials records what was tried without them.

lessons.title: A detector that cries wolf gets deleted; filter, ratchet, and separate the unresolvable
lessons.text: A check that produces false alarms trains everyone to ignore it. New checks filter known-safe shapes, freeze existing debt as a baseline that must not grow, and separate "confirmed" from "could not tell".

lessons.title: Vendor-side change is invisible from inside the repository
lessons.text: A vendor can retire an identifier your code hardcodes while every test passes. External identifiers live in one place, never as moving aliases, and a scheduled job asks the vendor whether each still exists.

lessons.title: Walk the user-type matrix before calling a user-facing change done
lessons.text: A change tested only as a brand-new user can exclude everyone who already exists. Each user population — new, existing, offline, interrupted, returning — is walked before a change is called done.

lessons.title: Verify a security claim against every file the setting can live in
lessons.text: One-click "always allow" answers accumulate into standing permissions nobody remembers granting. Grants are audited across every file they can live in, and destructive operations carry an explicit deny.

lessons.title: Preserve raw intake; archive by moving with links that resolve, never by tombstone or alias
lessons.text: A knowledge base is archived by moving, never by leaving stubs that compete with live notes, and raw material that a pass cannot read is kept and handed forward, never deleted.

lessons.title: Fixed-slot schedules starve on a machine that is often off
lessons.text: A job scheduled for a fixed hour on a machine that may be asleep can miss forever. Scheduled work polls frequently, gates on a success stamp, and writes evidence on every run so a dead job cannot pass as a quiet one.

lessons.title: A diagnostic is read-only; a health check that mutates misclassifies work
lessons.text: A health check that also cleans up will eventually delete work it misjudged. Diagnostics only report; any mutation is a separate, deliberate command.

lessons.title: A gate that can never pass is worse than no gate
lessons.text: A check that has never passed is not protecting anything; it is teaching people to ignore red. Every gate has a green in its history or it is fixed or removed.

lessons.title: Removing a control is only safe once you know which mechanism was the control
lessons.text: "Remove the guardrail" names an effect, not a file — list every mechanism producing that effect and split enforcement from detection before deleting one of them.

lessons.title: A monitor's silence is a finding; publish the silence, not the last verdict
lessons.text: A monitor that stops running looks exactly like a calm week; make the age of the data a reported number, and let it outrank the verdict.

lessons.title: A lesson written at one call site is not a fix
lessons.text: Two tools that talk to the same API should share the code that signs the request, or the second one will meet a quirk the first already learned.

lessons.title: "Shipped" must mean reached people, not reached a lane
lessons.text: A build that reached your test track has not shipped. Measure the distance between where a release stopped and where your customers are.

lessons.title: A safe ceiling nothing opts into is a bug wearing a feature's clothes
lessons.text: A safety ceiling that nothing switches on protects nobody. When a config value has both a conservative default and a documented safe maximum, verify in production that something actually requests the maximum — don't assume the default was meant to be temporary just because a comment says so.

lessons.title: A percentage cannot say "broken" from "nothing to measure"
lessons.text: A conversion rate with no population behind it is not a zero — report what could be measured, what could not, and why, as three different answers, not one misleading percentage.

lessons.title: A rule that reads the old document must constrain the new one
lessons.text: A security rule that only says who may write, while the server later trusts what was written, lets the subject of a decision author its inputs. Write rules constrain the new document, not just the identity making the change.

lessons.title: A config value the platform will refuse is not configured
lessons.text: A config value your tool accepts can still be refused by the program that actually reads it, and a daemon keeps the copy it read at startup.

lessons.title: A monitor that can only say "finding" or "silence" cannot report its own illness
lessons.text: A check that reports only problems cannot tell you it stopped working. Make it prove it ran, and test it against an example it should fail.

lessons.title: Tune the threshold only after you can defend the evidence selector
lessons.text: Pick what proves the job ran before arguing about how long is too long. A proxy anyone else can touch stops proving anything the moment they do.

lessons.title: Scheduled work competes for your interactive quota, and it always loses
lessons.text: Scheduled automation and your own heavy usage can draw on one budget. The schedule loses, quietly, and its status may still read as success.

lessons.title: A platform enforces its own operation model, not the one your comment describes
lessons.text: A permission protects the operation the platform thinks you performed, not the one the comment above it names. Replacing a stored file can count as creating it, so a rule that restricts updates may leave content wide open — and because the rule and its comment agree with each other, review cannot see it. Settle each boundary by making the request and watching which rule answers.

lessons.title: A fixture that disagrees with production about a field's TYPE tests the fixture
lessons.text: Databases that sort values by type quietly return nothing when a query's value is the wrong type — no error, just an empty result. Tests miss it when their sample data uses the type the code expects rather than the type the database holds. Worse, code syncing server state against local state reads that empty answer as a deletion and discards good data.

lessons.title: A counter that increments on ATTEMPT will report a healthy system that delivers nothing
lessons.text: If you count messages when you try to send them rather than when they arrive, your dashboard stays green while nobody hears from you — and any rule like "skip the email, we already sent a notification" starts silencing the one channel that still works. Record what was delivered, make the skip rule depend on it, and when that logic breaks let it send twice rather than stay quiet.

lessons.title: An element that captures taps must never need an animation to become visible
lessons.text: An invisible overlay that still catches taps is among the worst bugs an interface can have: everything looks fine, nothing responds, and people assume the app is broken and leave. Anything covering the screen should be visible the moment it appears; animate only the content inside it.

lessons.title: Registering a resource in one place leaves it invisible to the thing that starts it
lessons.text: A job registered where it is defined but not where it is started never runs, and waiting forever looks exactly like a slow machine.

lessons.title: "any" is not "all", and a fleet health check that ORs reports green until the last member dies
lessons.text: A health check that asks "is any of it alive" will report green until the last one dies. If you meant all of them, count them.

lessons.title: Being thorough on the same box as the thing you are waiting for is a way of breaking it
lessons.text: Running your own thorough checks on the machine that is already busy finishing the job can be the thing that fails it.

lessons.title: A liveness check must identify the holder, not its species
lessons.text: Code that waits for a lock first asks whether whoever holds it is still running. If that check looks for "a process like the holder" rather than the exact one, it matches the asker itself, decides the dead holder is alive, and waits forever. Record the holder's process id and ask about that. And if something else is timing you, give up before it does.

lessons.title: an id you never check for uniqueness is not an id
lessons.text: If your records are keyed by a number someone types, check that no two records share one. Checks that look at each record separately can never catch it, and a duplicate can quietly inherit the original's passing grade.

lessons.title: A document that records its own supersession contains both answers
lessons.text: Documents keep their own history, so the old answer and the new one sit in the same sentence. Any tool reading that text has to know which is current, and should say "I don't know" rather than quietly using the old one.

lessons.title: A default nobody declares is a resource everybody claims
lessons.text: Tools pick defaults, so every project that does not choose a port or a path takes the same one. It works until two run together, and then the second one can quietly take over the first one's data rather than simply failing. Name the defaults, and have something check that no two projects chose alike.

lessons.title: Merged is not deployed; ask production what it is running
lessons.text: Shipping code to the main branch is not the same as running it. Every backend needs something that deploys on merge and then asks the live system what it is actually running — comparing content, not timestamps, because a redeploy of identical files looks like a change and is not one.

lessons.title: A cache on a persistent runner is a tax, not a cache
lessons.text: A build cache only helps when the machine forgets between runs. On a machine that remembers, it adds a slow upload of files already sitting there — and because that cost lands after the tests pass, the job gets killed at its time limit with a perfectly green log, which looks like flakiness rather than configuration.

lessons.title: An edit that parses is not an edit that applied; read the value back
lessons.text: In configuration files a repeated setting usually means the last one wins, so adding a line above an existing block can quietly change nothing at all — the file still parses and the change still looks right when reviewed. Read the value back after editing, and be careful that the tool you check with is not the one performing the overwrite.

lessons.title: A credential fallback hides a dead credential; fail instead
lessons.text: If a job says it runs as a particular identity, make something in it actually use that identity and fail when it cannot. Tools quietly fall back to whatever login they can find, so a dead credential can sit unnoticed for months behind a wall of successful runs.

lessons.title: An empty 2xx is not content; check the body before diagnosing the layer above it
lessons.text: A 200 with no body is a failure wearing a success code; check what came back before deciding what broke.

lessons.title: A healthy app endpoint says nothing about its identity provider
lessons.text: A product can be online while its sign-in provider rejects every user.

lessons.title: Credential ignore rules must name the formats people actually download
lessons.text: Ignore credential files using the extensions vendors actually deliver,

lessons.title: A fix written next to one call site is invisible at the next one
lessons.text: A fix applied by hand at one call site is a patch, not a rule — write the scanner that would have caught the second occurrence in the same file.

lessons.title: A credential rotation is not done until the old credential is disabled
lessons.text: Finishing a credential rotation means disabling the old credential in

lessons.title: A shared runner is a shared resource; capacity is a class of incident, and a split runner splits shared baselines too
lessons.text: When you move CI off a saturated shared runner, keep every trigger of a workflow that carries pixel-exact baselines on the same environment — or the fix itself becomes a new source of false reds.

lessons.title: Every runtime that holds a copy of a secret needs a drift check
lessons.text: A secret copied into several runtimes can go stale in any one of them;

lessons.title: A shared staleness clock attributes drift to whatever changed last, correctly or not
lessons.text: A monitor that watches several things under one trigger must time each one against its own evidence — otherwise an edit to your neighbor reads as proof that you changed.

lessons.title: A lockfile regenerated on one OS can silently drop the binaries another OS builds with
lessons.text: A lockfile shared by several operating systems is only checked by the one CI runs on; test that it still carries the native pieces the other builds need, or the least frequent build finds out first.

lessons.title: Never let an agent print a secret value; assume every command trace and config-read response is live until proven otherwise
lessons.text: Agents should never print a secret's value, even from an operation labeled read-only; browser snapshots, debug traces, and config responses can carry live credentials without anyone intending it.

lessons.title: A release lane that orders steps differently from CI is a different environment; reproduce its order before shipping
lessons.text: A release pipeline that runs steps in a different order from CI is a different environment, so reproduce its order before trusting a green CI run.

lessons.title: A release step that changes a value must update what checks that value in the same commit
lessons.text: If a release step changes a value a separate check verifies, update that check's target in the very same commit — otherwise the next unrelated change is the one that gets blamed for the drift.

lessons.title: Verify a deploy the way a user fetches it
lessons.text: Check a deploy the way your users fetch it. A cache in the middle can hand a command-line check the new file and every visitor the old one.

lessons.title: Every branch of an update handler ends in a navigation
lessons.text: An update button that can finish without moving the user to the new version is broken, even when it never throws.

lessons.title: A gate's answer is its own exit status, and an empty answer is not green
lessons.text: Check the gate's own exit code before you merge. A pipe can turn a failed check into a green light, and an empty status list is not a pass.

lessons.title: One authority per topic; a retired competitor is deleted, not archived
lessons.text: Give every topic exactly one home and delete the copies; an archived duplicate still misleads whoever searches for it next.

lessons.title: A promise is not an answer, and a pending list has no window
lessons.text: Record "I will do it" separately from "it is done", and never let a request leave the open list on a promise. Show an unanswered reply before asking the person to decide again.

lessons.title: A failed sync cannot be followed by a push
lessons.text: Verify the branch, history and remote commit before a shared sync claims success or starts the work it recorded.

lessons.title: Shared writers need a schedule and a bounded lock wait
lessons.text: Stagger shared jobs and verify each scheduled run, rather than treating a skipped lock attempt as a successful update.

lessons.title: Browser readback is not safe on a credential dashboard
lessons.text: Inspect broker state through authenticated API reads, and rotate any credential that appears in a chat or tool transcript.

lessons.title: Keep operational failures separate from admitted commitments
lessons.text: Preserve operational failures without letting each event create a new commitment; use an explicit admission gate for durable work.

lessons.title: A rotation is not finished until every copy is proven equal
lessons.text: After rotating a credential, verify by hash that every stored copy matches the new value instead of assuming the sync reached them.

lessons.title: The runtime checkout must be clean main, and something must say so
lessons.text: Scheduled jobs should run from a checkout that is verified to be on the current main branch, and a monitor should flag any drift.

lessons.title: Customers get a stable build; a measurement window freezes the product
lessons.text: A product that changes every day cannot be measured. Ship customer-facing changes in batches, and freeze everything but core-path repairs while a test is running.

lessons.title: Monitor the core path with a real transaction, never a preflight
lessons.text: A preflight or a health check can be green while the product's main action fails for every user. Monitor the path that matters with a real, synthetic transaction in production.

lessons.title: Prove day-1 return before buying traffic
lessons.text: Paid traffic tells you whether you can buy users, not whether they want the product. Prove that people come back on their own before paying for more of them.

lessons.title: One owner metric per product, fixed before spending
lessons.text: Pick the one number that decides a product before spending money on it, compute it daily with a script, and do not swap it for a friendlier number when it disappoints.

lessons.title: A kill rule names a dollar ceiling that trips without a meeting
lessons.text: A kill rule without a dollar limit gets extended one more week at a time. Write the spend ceiling and the revenue floor into the rule, and pause spend automatically when the ceiling is crossed.

lessons.title: Add a platform only with its own core-path monitor and release path
lessons.text: Every platform you ship on is another product to keep working. Make the core loop solid on one platform first, and add another only when it has its own monitoring and release path.

lessons.title: Gate a VM's work on the host resource that kills it
lessons.text: Watch the resource that actually takes the machine down. A virtual machine with plenty of memory still dies when the disk under it fills.

lessons.title: A lifecycle that deletes files must update every guard that tests for them
lessons.text: When a cleanup deletes files, update every check that looked for them, or something will helpfully recreate what you just removed.

lessons.title: A watcher cannot run on the scheduler it watches
lessons.text: A monitor that runs on the system it watches goes quiet exactly when that system dies. Give the scheduler a heartbeat that something else checks.

lessons.title: An admission gate should queue work, not fail it
lessons.text: A queue that gives up on waiting jobs turns a busy system into a broken one. Keep the safety limits fixed and let the line be long.

lessons.title: Merge append-only files as a union; refuse conflicts everywhere else
lessons.text: When two sides only ever append, a conflict is not a disagreement. Keep both, and save the hard stop for files where it means something.

lessons.title: A catch-all that maps every verification error to "unauthenticated" hides outages
lessons.text: An error handler that treats every failure as "signed out" turns an outage into a quiet login prompt. Test the signed-in path, not just the front door.

lessons.title: Strip control markup at the boundary that publishes, not where it is written
lessons.text: If a document mixes what readers see with internal switches, the publishing step has to strip the switches. Trusting every writer to put them in the right place eventually shows them to readers.

lessons.title: A forwarder is unconfirmed until a message has gone through it
lessons.text: A forwarding rule is only a claim until a test message has actually come out the other side, so test it on a schedule.

lessons.title: A cleanup must name what it may never touch
lessons.text: A cleanup that decides what is finished by its shape will eventually delete something live, so it needs an explicit list of things it may never touch, plus an alarm when one of them disappears.

lessons.title: Meet the intent before writing an owner card
lessons.text: Before asking a person to do a task, try two different ways to meet its intent yourself; a forgotten password can usually be reset rather than recovered.

lessons.title: A platform's default grant is a decision nobody made
lessons.text: Database functions that run with elevated rights are only as safe as the list of who may call them, and platform defaults often say "everyone", so that list has to be set on purpose and checked continuously.

lessons.title: A trading host's clock is an input; measure it
lessons.text: Systems that judge data freshness by the local clock need that clock watched too; a few seconds of drift can look exactly like stale data.

lessons.title: Fix generated code at its source, never in the copy
lessons.text: Code generated from a shared source is fixed in that source and re-synced; a check flags any copy that no longer matches its release.

lessons.title: Asking a tool for help must never run it
lessons.text: Asking a release script for help must never run the release; scripts default to a dry run, and a sandboxed test proves every help call is inert.

lessons.title: The routes the law requires get a production probe too
lessons.text: Deleting your account is checked daily in production with a throwaway account, so a broken deletion path pages someone instead of waiting for a user to find it.

lessons.title: A cap must hold after the action, not only before it
lessons.text: A limit that is only compared with where you are now, and not with where the next step takes you, lets a single step jump past it.

lessons.title: A suite that reads the clock must also run when the clock is unkind
lessons.text: A test that only passes at certain hours is a clock check, not a test; run the suite at the bad hour on purpose.

lessons.title: Test motion with motion on; animate only what the user caused
lessons.text: An animation test suite that runs with animations turned off proves nothing about motion. Only animate what the user's own tap caused.

lessons.title: Read-only git calls under a kill timeout must not take locks
lessons.text: A health check that gets killed partway through can leave behind the very lock that then blocks everything else. Make read-only checks lock-free.

lessons.title: Check a repository's integrity before writing to it
lessons.text: Automated writers sharing a git repository should check its integrity before each write. Repair automatically only what cannot lose data, and stop everything else until a person looks.

lessons.title: Never pass a secret on a command line
lessons.text: Never put a secret on a command line. Every user on the machine can read process arguments, so pass secrets through the environment or a file instead.

lessons.title: A default release command must never reach production
lessons.text: The everyday release command should only ever ship to testers. Shipping to real users should take a separate, deliberate step that promotes the exact build that was already tested.

lessons.title: Audit traffic shares the CI runner's IP; a 403 challenge is not a regression
lessons.text: If your test runner and your audit tooling leave the network from the same address, a bot shield will eventually block them both at once. Teach the test suite to tell "the host is blocking me" apart from "the site is broken."

lessons.title: A watchdog on a log's mtime proves the job ran, not that it worked
lessons.text: A backup monitor should alert on the last success, not on the last activity, or it will stay green through repeated failures.

lessons.title: Live state with one copy is an incident waiting; back up databases with the database
lessons.text: Copy a live database with its own backup tool and verify the copy, because a plain file copy of a database in use can be silently corrupt.
